source: Veinott and Lehman (2024) Adaptive Planning: Comparing Human and AI Responses in Premortem Planning (abstract page)
finding: The only located LLM-vs-human premortem paper. It is a qualitative comparison of student-written failure reasons with ChatGPT-4 failure reasons for the same plan. The abstract page gives no results, so whether LLM causes matched human causes is still unknown.
numbers: No numbers on the page. Pages 256-268, HCII 2024 Late Breaking Papers, 38 references.
quote: compared reasons for plan failure written by students with reasons generated by a large language model (ChatGPT-4)
limits: Springer full text redirects to a login wall; not read. Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open. Do not cite any similarity or difference claim. The design (qualitative, not scored against confirmed flaws) could not answer our test anyway.

finding: Crossref confirms authors, venue and page range. It has no abstract and no results text.
agent_relevance: Confirms the paper exists; adds nothing on results.

source: Mitchell, Russo, Pennington (1989) Back to the future: Temporal perspective in the explanation of events (abstract via Crossref)
finding: The abstract does not report the oft-cited +30%. Experiment 1 found that temporal perspective (future vs past) had little influence. What mattered was outcome certainty: explanations for sure events were longer, held a higher share of episodic reasons and were written in past tense. Experiment 2 says uncertainty changes the type of explanation, not the time spent.
numbers: No N, test statistics or percentages in the abstract.
quote: temporal perspective showed little influence while outcome uncertainty strongly affected the nature of explanations
limits: Abstract only (paywalled full text). The +30% (a count of reasons, per Klein 2007) is still unverified in the primary, and the abstract points to certainty, not hindsight direction, as the active ingredient.
agent_relevance: Treat the failure frame as a certainty manipulation. In an agent prompt the factor to test is 'state that failure is certain', not 'pretend it is the future'. Do not use +30% as a prior.

source: Hill (2012) Cognition in the woods: Biases in probability judgments by search and rescue planners. Judgment and Decision Making 7(4), 488-498
finding: This is NOT a premortem study. It tests support-theory unpacking with 32 male search planners. Listing the five scenarios in which the lost person left the area (unpacking the residual hypothesis) raised the probability of 'outside the area' versus unpacking the focal hypothesis. The paper only cites Mitchell 1989, Koriat 1980 and Veinott 2010 in its discussion as work finding that prospective hindsight lowers overconfidence. Later reviews that cite Hill for reduced overconfidence cite a paper that did not test it.
numbers: N=32. Change-score test F(1,28)=4.753, p=.038, partial eta squared=.145. Only 11 of 32 subjects (34%) showed an unpacking effect. Residual group raised 'rest of world' estimate by over 4%; focal group lowered it by nearly 3%. Pre-manipulation means: .80 search area, .17 rest of world.
quote: This 'what if I'm wrong?' approach to decision making is similar to the so-called 'crystal ball' technique
limits: Single small vignette, all male, no outcome truth, no premortem condition. Experienced planners were if anything more likely to show unpacking.
agent_relevance: Correct b08/K02: remove Hill 2012 as premortem evidence. It does support a mechanism: listing failure scenarios inflates the judged chance of failure.

finding: Unpacking any hypothesis made the parts sum to more than the whole (subadditivity). Hill also warns that forced failure thinking could push people into underconfidence in the focal hypothesis and make planners abandon a good plan too soon.
numbers: Focal group: summed segment probability M=1.07 (SD .33) vs original .82 (SD .14), t(15)=3.14, p=.007. Residual group: M=.72 (SD .58) vs original .19 (SD .13), t(15)=3.72, p=.002. Difference in increase between groups (.52 vs .25) not significant, t(30)=1.61, p=.118.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation for gap 6: part of any premortem confidence drop is generic listing/unpacking inflation, not insight. Control arm needed: list N success scenarios vs N failure scenarios at equal tokens. Also measure over-correction (good answers abandoned).

source: Park, Lu, Hedgcock (2017) Relative effects of forward and backward planning on goal pursuit. Psychological Science 28, 1620-1630 (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Planning steps backward from the goal beat forward planning on motivation, goal expectancy, less felt time pressure and goal-relevant performance. The effect ran through clearer task representation and was strongest when goals were complex to plan. A corrigendum was published in 2018 (DOI 10.1177/0956797617752922); its content was not read.
numbers: No N or effect sizes in the abstract.
quote: backward planning allowed people to think of tasks required to reach their goals more clearly, especially when goals were complex to plan
limits: Abstract only; Sage page returned 403. Backward PLANNING is not backward EXPLANATION of failure, so it is only an analogue. The corrigendum may change numbers.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 half open. Supports a 'work backward from the end state' step on complex plans, with a complexity condition (matches Peabody Exp 3). Do not cite magnitudes.

source: Roose, Lehman, Veinott (2023) Premortems in Game Development Teams: Impact and Potential. HFES Annual Meeting (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Ten game teams (68 members) ran one premortem early in a year-long project. They named many failure reasons and mitigations, but surprisingly few teams revised their plans to cut complexity. There was no comparison condition, so no premortem benefit is shown.
numbers: 10 teams, n=68. Mean 17.8 unique failure reasons and 16.7 mitigations per team.
limits: Abstract only. No control arm, no outcome measure. Counts of reasons say nothing about correctness.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: Roose gives no benefit evidence. It shows the premortem's weak link: finding causes is easy, acting on them is not. Our scaffold must force a plan-revision step and test it.

source: Zhang et al. (2023, J Personality) Future-oriented temporal perspective promotes wise reasoning (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Cited in a 2025 premortem review as support. It is not a premortem study. People reasoning about their own interpersonal conflicts from a future viewpoint showed more wise reasoning than from the present, strongest at 30 years ahead.
numbers: 3 experiments, total N=622. Self-report and open-ended wise-reasoning measures.
limits: Abstract only. Interpersonal conflicts, not plans; no failure framing; no accuracy outcome.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: Zhang shows no premortem benefit. At most it says viewing from a distance may widen reasoning; treat as a weak analogy.

source: Peabody (thesis) Improving Planning: Quantitative Evaluation of the Premortem Technique in Field and Laboratory Settings, Michigan Tech
finding: The repository page dates the thesis 2017 (earlier notes said 2022). Exp 1: 52 Army cadets in teams, timed field exercises; premortem teams made fewer errors and showed less fixation, no change in planning or execution time. Exp 2: 72 individuals, premortem vs worst-case method gave similar counts of reasons and solutions but different categories. Exp 3: 82 participants on a complex, unfamiliar plan; premortem produced more reasons; groups produced more solutions than individuals.
numbers: N=52, 72, 82 confirmed from the abstract. No test statistics or effect sizes seen.
limits: Abstract only; PDF blocked by a bot check (not bypassed). The date mismatch with earlier notes is unresolved.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 partly closed: the 'helps only on complex unfamiliar plans' reading rests on Exp 2 (equal counts) vs Exp 3 (more), counts only. Run our own test: premortem vs worst-case prompt on easy vs hard items, log token cost.

source: InvThink: Premortem Reasoning for Safer Language Models, arXiv 2510.01569v3 (full PDF text)
finding: A prompting and training method: list possible harms, analyse their consequences, then answer under mitigation constraints. The prompt-only version beat zero-shot, CoT and a plain safety instruction on judged harmfulness. The plain safety instruction used similar token counts and did worse, so structured failure listing beat an unstructured 'be safe' instruction.
numbers: TRIDENT mean harmfulness (1-5, lower better): zero-shot 3.22, SafetyPrompt 2.62, InvThink 2.19 (32% less than zero-shot). SafetyBench gain about 5-13%; Illegal Activities +15.8% (N=1,767). Prompt-only InvThink cut blackmail rates 90% and murder-attempt rates 44% on average. Judges: Gemini-2.5 Pro, o3-mini, Claude 3.7 Sonnet; inter-judge Pearson r=0.819.
quote: merely instructing models to "be safe" is insufficient
limits: Safety domain, not reasoning accuracy. LLM judges. Open models 0.27B-72B plus some proprietary models in an appendix. Authors' own benchmark framing (TRIDENT).
agent_relevance: Gap 2 evidence: a failure-first structure beat a plain instruction at similar tokens, but the target is harm avoidance, not flaws confirmed by a check. Needs a reasoning-accuracy replication.

source: InvThink appendix B.2: controlled isolation of trace direction (PROTHINK forward control)
finding: The authors trained one model on harm enumeration (inverse) and another on the same targets rewritten as positive-goal enumeration (forward), matching prompts, depth and tokens. The two were statistically indistinguishable on safety. They call this a null result for direction at the SFT stage.
numbers: Qwen-2.5-7B, 23,063 training targets. TRIDENT safety rate 1.000 both; avg harmfulness 1.23 (inverse) vs 1.01 (forward). StrongREJECT attack success 0.000 both. XSTest false-refusal rate 0.980 both (both collapse to refusal).
quote: trace direction does not differentiate safety behavior at the SFT stage
limits: SFT only, one model, refusal-only data, so both arms collapsed to refusing; the test had little power to separate them. No prompt-only forward control reported.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the only LLM test of direction found. Null. Our prompt-time arms need a forward 'list success scenarios' control at equal tokens before we credit the failure frame.

source: InvThink Table 5: reasoning accuracy of Qwen3-8B variants
finding: After InvThink training the model kept or slightly raised reasoning scores. The authors guess that listing failure modes makes the model check constraints, but give no test of that. They say differences on GPQA and MATH500 come from a single seed and should be read with care.
numbers: Qwen3-8B average over GPQA, MATH500, ARC-C, MMLU: base 0.61, general SFT 0.56, InvThink SFT 0.61, RL 0.60, SFT+RL 0.63. MATH500: base 0.50, SFT+RL 0.55. GPQA 0.46 to 0.51. TRIDENT harmfulness 3.12 to 1.22.
limits: Trained model, not a scaffold. Single seed. Gains of 2-5 points may be inside noise.
agent_relevance: No evidence that a prompt-time premortem raises math or logic accuracy. Do not claim it.

source: AUGUR: Proactive Failure Anticipation for Reliable LLM Reasoning (preprint, Oct 2026; abstract via Crossref)
finding: A pre-mortem reasoning framework trained with a failure-aware supervised cold start plus GRPO with rewards for anticipating failure and verifying. It beats GRPO baselines on math benchmarks.
limits: Abstract only (full text returned 403). Trained, not a prompt. The abstract shows no prompt-only pre-mortem arm and no equal-token control. Preprint, not peer reviewed.
agent_relevance: Weak support that anticipating failure points plus naming a verification strategy can help math when trained. For a scaffold, the useful part is probably 'name a check', not the imagery.

source: Prospective Hindsight: Self-Calibrating Reinforcement Learning via Prediction-Reality Gaps, arXiv 2610.02740 (abstract)
finding: Name collision, not a premortem. The method weights RL advantages by the gap between an agent's prediction before feedback and its evaluation after. It reports better task performance and calibration; miscalibration shifts from overconfident failures (single-turn) to underconfident successes (multi-turn).
limits: Abstract only (via search listing). Training method.
agent_relevance: Do not count this as premortem evidence. The underconfidence finding is a reminder that any confidence-lowering step can overshoot (see the Hill 2012 caveat).

source: Ghosh, Sarkar, Lindley, Poelitz (2026) Experimental Comparison of Cognitive Forcing Functions for Execution Plans in AI-Assisted Writing, arXiv 2601.18033 (page text, partly read)
finding: Humans reviewing GPT-4o plans with seeded errors. An 'Assumptions' check cut overreliance without raising load. A 'WhatIf' (failure-style hypothesis) prompt was rated more helpful but did not measure better. Both together may be ineffective or harmful.
numbers: Main study N=214 (groups 60, 45, 50, 59); interviews N=12; four seeded error types. Odds ratios not read (page truncated).
limits: Human reviewers of AI output, not an LLM running the premortem. Only the first ~100k characters read.
agent_relevance: Supports gaps 6 and 10: what feels useful (what-if) can differ from what catches errors, and stacking prompts can backfire. Score our arms by caught flaws, never by self-reported usefulness.

source: Investigating how people use ChatGPT for long-term life task planning, arXiv 2512.11096
finding: Interview study, no failure-prompt arm. Participants saw ChatGPT's success-oriented tone hide signs of possible failure and encourage overconfidence. The authors recommend failure-oriented planning support but did not test it.
numbers: N=14 (7 mailing list, 7 Reddit). Refinement requests 24 times, verification requests 15 times.
agent_relevance: Default LLM planning is success-framed. A built-in failure step is a design gap, not a tested fix.

source: When Do Audited Action Gates Help? The Cost and Failure Conditions of Epistemic Strictness in LLM Agents (SSRN 7348298, abstract via Crossref)
finding: Closest located test for gap 4 (verified vs unverified claims). Agents' own labels of 'verified' were unreliable: they marked rules verified that were never tested by intervention. A gate that trusted those labels gave no detectable benefit. A harness-audited gate did help downstream diagnosis, though the abstract says the benefit was concentrated (text cut off). Stricter gates also lowered discovery of true rules.
numbers: 1,330 runs, nine models. Spurious-rule adoption down 1.51 of 4; true-rule recall down 0.111 (paired n=57, Holm p<0.02). Audited gate improved diagnosis by +0.114 [+0.019, +0.208] (n=55 paired, four models, held-out half).
limits: Abstract snippet only; synthetic fault-diagnosis environment; not a premortem. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Supports: do not let the model self-certify its causes; keep only causes a harness or tool confirms. Expect a recall cost.

source: Gaps 2, 5, 8: search record for LLM premortem confidence and diversity studies
finding: arXiv listing for 'premortem' returned 6 records; only InvThink (2510.01569) tests a premortem on LLMs. Others: a tutorial (2609.22249, lists premortems among prompting techniques, not benchmarked), a uniqueness-bias paper (2408.07710, 219 projects, premortem named as a mitigation), and unrelated items. Searches for 'pre-mortem' and 'prospective hindsight' found only d13 and d14. No study found that (a) compares a failure-frame prompt with a plain risk-list prompt on current reasoning models at equal tokens, (b) measures P(True) shift after a premortem, or (c) measures diversity of repeated premortem samples.
limits: Not exhaustive: the arXiv API and search page returned 429 repeatedly, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited, the WebSearch budget ran out after 1 call, and Crossref keyword search is noisy. The listing was summarised by a fetch model.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2, 5, 8 stay open and are original experiments for our bench: equal-token arms, P(True) before and after, k-sample dedup counts.

source: Gallop and Bischoff (2016) How to catch a black swan: Measuring the benefits of the premortem technique for risk identification (Crossref record)
finding: Record exists (Journal of Enterprise Transformation). Crossref gives no abstract, so N=101 and the claimed benefits remain second-hand.
agent_relevance: Do not cite K04 numbers as verified.
